When found Usually localized Usually widespread Where it starts Central nodes you can't see: in the chest, by the heart, in the lungs, or possibly the abdomen Peripheral nodes, or outside the nodes Spread Contiguous: from one node to the node next to it Can be non-contiguous: a node above the diaphragm and one below, with the node between them not enlarged Outside the nodes Uncommon Much more common Peripheral blood Never involved Can be involved The tumor cells A few scattered, very abnormal, bizarre cells, so it can be tricky to diagnose Look very much like normal lymphocytes, so the tests are put together Treatment ABVD Often CHOP He said the main Hodgkin lymphoma is classic Hodgkin lymphoma: "You don't need to know the non-classical." It is different from the rest. The tumor cells are a small fraction of the mass, sparse and very large, embedded in a reactive background rich in immune cells. They are the Hodgkin cells (one nucleus) and the Reed-Sternberg cells (two or more nuclei), together called HRS cells. The classic Reed-Sternberg cell has two nuclear lobes, each with a prominent, eosinophilic (pink) nucleolus, which gives it an owl's-eye look. "That's the main thing that you need to recognize, is those Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells." Lymphoid blasts do not have Auer rods." The gonads, as a site outside the marrow, are more specific to ALL, and flow cytometry tells the two apart, by markers you don't need. 6 Chronic myeloid leukemia, the chronic leukemia he said to know: BCR-ABL1 and the Philadelphia chromosome, a very high count with every stage of maturation and few blasts, imatinib Study guide + recording · 3 questions in the bank Know this CML: t(9;22), the Philadelphia chromosome and BCR-ABL1; a very high white count with every stage of maturation and few blasts; tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib. Its blood and marrow. The white count is high, from 12,000 to 1,000,000 per microliter, with a median of about 80,000 (the slide writes it as 12 to 1,000 times 10 to the 9th per liter). The cells are mostly neutrophils at every stage of maturation, with peaks at the myelocytes and the segmented neutrophils, not blasts. He put it as the full pattern of maturation, from early blasts all the way to neutrophils, all increased in the blood and the marrow, with a count high enough to separate it from a reactive one, such as an infection. The marrow is hypercellular, more than 95 percent cellular, with granulocytes at every stage, and his slide shows small, hypolobated megakaryocytes. The karyotype shows the Philadelphia chromosome. Its treatment. Knowing the abnormal signal led to drugs that block it, the tyrosine kinase inhibitors, of which imatinib (Gleevec) was the first and is first-line therapy. It targets the enzymatically active part of the p210 BCR-ABL1 protein: it competes with ATP for the active site and so prevents the kinase from activating. He put it as blocking the binding site, so BCR-ABL1 can't bind its substrate and drive the cell to proliferate. In this era of kinase inhibitors, the most important sign of prognosis is the response to treatment, measured in the blood count, the chromosomes and the molecular test. 7 CLL/SLL: one disease of small, mature B cells, named by where it is (blood or node); soccer-ball chromatin and smudge cells; at least 5 times 10 to the 9th B cells per liter for CLL; older patients, infections, largely incurable Study guide + recording · 3 questions in the bank CLL is diagnosed from the blood: a B-cell count of at least 5 times 10 to the 9th per liter (5,000 per microliter), with the typical look and markers. The look, which his objective stresses "particularly in blood": small lymphocytes with clumped chromatin, a pattern compared to cracked mud or a soccer ball, and many smudge cells, fragile lymphocytes that have burst apart as the smear is made. "That's a clue right away, I'm looking at that, I'm thinking CLL." The marrow can be involved in various patterns, which he said you don't need to know. In a lymph node the small cells infiltrate diffusely, with pale areas of larger cells called proliferation centers. 8 Burkitt lymphoma: very aggressive and very fast-growing, t(8;14) and MYC, the starry sky of macrophages eating debris, the jaw, EBV, and excellent survival with chemotherapy Study guide + recording · 4 questions in the bank Know this Burkitt lymphoma's starry sky is macrophages eating the debris of tumor cells that proliferate very fast; it carries t(8;14), MYC with IGH. Under the microscope: sheets of uniform, medium-sized, cohesive blue cells, with many tingible-body macrophages scattered among them. These macrophages have eaten the debris of tumor cells that died by apoptosis, and their pale cytoplasm against the dark blue sheet gives the classic starry-sky pattern, which he compared to Van Gogh's painting and called "the key morphologic finding in making this diagnosis". With modern immunochemotherapy including rituximab, in high-resource settings, the prognosis is excellent: overall survival over 90 percent in children and 80 percent in adults. He said that is why the diagnosis matters: the chemotherapy works. 9 Mantle cell lymphoma: from the follicle's mantle zone, t(11;14) (nothing else among the lymphomas carries it), the cyclin D1 stain, older adults with enlarged nodes, survival much longer than it was Study guide + recording · 3 questions in the bank Know this Cyclin D1, switched on by t(11;14), means mantle cell lymphoma; he said nothing else among the lymphomas carries t(11;14). Its genetic hallmark, and the first event in its development, is the translocation between chromosomes 11 and 14, t(11;14), present in at least 95 percent of cases. It switches on cyclin D1, and his slide calls the cyclin D1 stain diagnostic. He said the translocation "tells me right away, I'm looking at mantle cell lymphoma. Nothing else in the lymphomas will do that." Its cells carry CD5, like CLL/SLL's, so he needs another marker to tell them apart: cyclin D1, found by immunohistochemistry, not flow cytometry. "If you got a test question, let's say this is expressing cyclin D1, you would know this is mantle cell lymphoma." 10 Mycosis fungoides, the most common skin lymphoma, an indolent T-cell lymphoma (patches, then plaques, then tumors), and Sézary syndrome, its aggressive form (erythroderma, nodes and cerebriform Sézary cells in the blood) Study guide + recording · 2 questions in the bank He went through these quickly: "I'm not going to go over in much detail, but know that these are the most common types of cutaneous lymphomas that are involving the skin, and that they have an indolent course." Mycosis fungoides is a T-cell lymphoma of the skin; with Sézary syndrome it is the most common type of cutaneous lymphoma, more than half of cases. Its lesions evolve in sequence: patches, then plaques, then tumors. They can be one or many; when localized they favor sun-protected skin, the flexures (armpits and groin) and the lower trunk and buttocks, a "bathing-trunk" distribution. Under the microscope, small to medium-sized T cells with a clear halo and hyperchromatic, hyperconvoluted ("cerebriform") nuclei line up along the basal layer and infiltrate the epidermis: they are epidermotropic. The course is indolent, over years or decades, with lesions that persist and grow slowly. It can appear at any age, peaking in the late fifties. Sézary syndrome is defined by a triad: erythroderma (red skin over most of the body), generalized lymphadenopathy, and clonal T cells with cerebriform nuclei, Sézary cells, in the skin, the lymph nodes and the peripheral blood. He called it the aggressive version, with the blood and the nodes involved; the cerebriform nuclei in the blood help confirm it, and the node involvement can be subtle. Unlike mycosis fungoides, it is aggressive: the 5-year survival is 10 to 30 percent, and most patients die of opportunistic infections. 11 The other B-cell lymphomas and their associations: follicular lymphoma's t(14;18) and BCL2, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (about 30 percent of adult lymphomas), and marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma, the one dentists will see most, with its infections and autoimmune links Study guide + recording · 4 questions in the bank Know this Marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma: indolent, in the salivary glands and ocular adnexa, linked to H. pylori, Chlamydia psittaci, Sjögren syndrome and Hashimoto thyroiditis, with lymphoepithelial lesions as its key finding. Acute monocytic leukemia can show outside the marrow in the mouth, as swollen gums infiltrated by leukemic cells. He named two acute leukemias "you need to know", and this is the first. Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) is a type of AML in which abnormal promyelocytes predominate. Its genetic hallmark is a balanced translocation between chromosomes 15 and 17, t(15;17), which fuses the promyelocytic leukemia gene, PML, with the retinoic acid receptor alpha gene, RARA. The fusion protein, PML-RARA (written with a double colon on the slides), causes the disease by impairing myeloid differentiation: maturation stops at the promyelocyte. Patients present with symptoms of their cytopenias, with disease outside the marrow, or both, and the oral cavity is one of those places. AML that forms a mass outside the marrow is called a myeloid sarcoma (extramedullary AML). In the mouth it shows as gingival hypertrophy: swollen gums infiltrated by leukemic cells. His slides cite two case reports, one of them a myeloid sarcoma of the mandibular gingiva that was the relapse of a treated AML. This is what his objective means by the extramedullary presentation of acute leukemia. He said a biopsy of those gums can look a little like lymphoma, but studies confirm the leukemia, and the marrow is diffusely full of blasts. 13 Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, only the gist he gave: very aggressive, B symptoms, a poor response to chemotherapy Study guide + recording · 1 question in the bank He skipped this slide ("I'm going to skip peripheral T-cell lymphoma"), giving only its gist: very aggressive T-cell lymphomas, whose markers say they are T cells, in patients who typically have B symptoms and don't necessarily respond to chemotherapy; the cells are large. The slide's detail follows. Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (PTCL, NOS) is a mixed category: the mature T-cell lymphomas, in nodes or outside them, that don't fit a specific type. It is diagnosed nearly always in adults, and most present with advanced disease, usually lymphadenopathy and B symptoms, often with the marrow, liver, spleen, skin or GI tract involved. It carries T-cell markers, more often CD4 than CD8. These are aggressive lymphomas, with a poor response to therapy, frequent relapses and low survival. 14 Lymphoma categories, his closing point: which lymphomas are B-cell and which T-cell, which are indolent and which aggressive, and the part of the follicle each B-cell lymphoma comes from Study guide + recording · 3 questions in the bank B-cell CLL/SLL, follicular lymphoma, mantle cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, Burkitt lymphoma T-cell or NK-cell Mycosis fungoides Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, Sézary syndrome, extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma 15 The B symptoms, his "high-yield clues" (a fever of 38 °C or more, drenching night sweats, losing 10 percent of body weight in 6 months): they raise the suspicion, and the tissue makes the diagnosis Recording + objectives · 2 questions in the bank Know this The B symptoms: a fever of 38 °C or higher, drenching night sweats that soak the sheets, and unexplained loss of at least 10 percent of body weight in 6 months; they raise the suspicion, and the tissue makes the diagnosis. Night sweats that soak the bedding and clothes: drenching sweats that make you change the sheets, not light ones Also flagged in class From Dr. Herr's study guide, for Dr. Borak's lecture. Place the four leukemias on two axes (acute or chronic, myeloid or lymphoid) and know each one's look: AML's blasts and Auer rods, ALL in young children, CML's Philadelphia chromosome, CLL's smudge cells. Know the two ways leukemia does harm (marrow failure: anemia, bleeding, infection; infiltration: spleen, liver, nodes, bone, gums), Hodgkin versus non-Hodgkin (Reed-Sternberg cells and contiguous nodes above the diaphragm, versus mostly B-cell and often extranodal), and the lymphomas by their associations: Burkitt (t(8;14), MYC, EBV, the jaw), mantle cell (t(11;14), cyclin D1), mycosis fungoides (patches, plaques, tumors) and Sézary syndrome (erythroderma, nodes, Sézary cells in the blood). Swollen gums from leukemic cells growing in them can be the first sign of a leukemia nobody has found yet; with fatigue, pallor and bruising, get a blood count. Blasts are the hallmark of acute leukemia, and more than 20 percent, in the blood or the marrow, makes the diagnosis; an AML with a defining genetic abnormality needs no set count. His closing summary: know each disease's category (B or T, indolent or aggressive, acute or chronic, myeloid or lymphoid) and its molecular association: t(14;18) follicular, t(11;14) mantle cell, t(8;14) Burkitt, t(9;22) CML, t(15;17) APL; not the markers. You can skip Skip the individual CD markers; know that flow cytometry reads the surface antigens to tell B, T or myeloid, mature or blast, and something abnormal, such as a clone with only kappa or only lambda. Skip the AML subtypes (M0 to M7) and the subtype lists of AML and ALL; know AML versus ALL, and the acute leukemias he named. Skip the differences between the classic Hodgkin subtypes (and the non-classical type, which he also said you don't need); recognize the Reed-Sternberg cells. Know only the gist he gave: a very aggressive T-cell lymphoma, usually with B symptoms, that doesn't necessarily respond to chemotherapy. Mycosis fungoides: know that it is the most common lymphoma of the skin, a T-cell lymphoma with an indolent course, and that Sézary syndrome is its aggressive form, with the blood and nodes involved. For B-ALL and T-ALL, know who gets them: mostly children (usually 1 to 5 years, poor prognosis under 1), less often adults; T-ALL is confirmed as T-cell by testing.
